title: Security Solutions, Detection Sources and Log Management
unit: CS-ICT251101 Monitor and Report Cyber Threats

parts.html:
At the end of this session, you should be able to:

  1. Describe the purpose of each security solution listed in the Competency Standards (AV, firewall, WAF, IDS/IPS, DLP, EDR/MDR, NDR, SIEM, SOAR, XDR, threat intelligence, OT and IoT security).
  2. Identify the source of a detection alert from its content.
  3. Explain how logs are generated, collected, normalized and stored in a SIEM.
  4. Interpret severity classifications used by security solutions.
  5. Read firewall and Windows security logs to find suspicious patterns.

Organizations use defense in depth — several security layers so that if one fails, another detects or stops the threat. Each layer is a potential source of detection alerts that you will monitor.

Security SolutionWhat It Protects / DoesTypical Alert
Anti-virus (AV)Scans files on endpoints for known malware signatures and heuristics"Trojan:Win32/Agent detected — quarantined"
Common firewallAllows/blocks traffic by IP, port, protocol"Denied inbound TCP 3389 from 192.0.2.8"
NGFWNext-generation firewall: firewall + application awareness + IPS"Blocked: known C2 application traffic"
WAFWeb Application Firewall — protects websites from SQL injection, XSS, etc."SQL injection attempt blocked on /login.php"
IDSIntrusion Detection System — watches traffic and alerts (does not block)"ET SCAN Nmap scan detected"
IPSIntrusion Prevention System — detects and blocks in-line"Exploit attempt dropped"
DLPData Loss Prevention — stops sensitive data leaving the organization"File with 200 credit card numbers sent to Gmail"
EDREndpoint Detection and Response — records endpoint behavior and can isolate hosts"Suspicious PowerShell spawned by Word"
MDRManaged Detection and Response — EDR/XDR operated by an outside providerProvider escalation email/call
NDRNetwork Detection and Response — analyzes network traffic behavior"Beaconing to rare external domain"
TDRThreat Detection and Response — platform detecting and responding across sourcesCorrelated threat case
SIEMSecurity Information and Event Management — collects and correlates logs from everything"Brute force followed by successful login"
SOARSecurity Orchestration, Automation and Response — automates playbooks"Playbook: phishing — URL blocked, ticket created"
XDRExtended Detection and Response — combines endpoint, network, email, cloud dataMulti-stage incident
Threat intelligenceFeeds of known-bad IPs, domains, hashes, actor information"Connection to IP on threat list"
OT/ICS/SCADA securityProtects industrial systems (power, water, manufacturing)"Unauthorized PLC write command"
IoT securityProtects smart devices (CCTV, sensors, smart TVs)"CCTV camera contacting unknown server"
NOTE — Detection alerts in the Competency Standards
The CS lists these alert sources: SIEM alert, AV alert, Firewall alert, Web application firewall alert, DLP alert, EDR alert and NDR alert.

A log is a time-stamped record of an event. A detection is a log or event that a security tool considers suspicious. Log management is the process of collecting, storing, protecting and reviewing logs.

The Log Pipeline

  1. Generate — devices (servers, endpoints, firewalls, applications) produce logs.
  2. Collect — logs are sent by agents (e.g., Wazuh agent, Winlogbeat) or via syslog to a collector.
  3. Normalize — different formats are converted into common fields (time, source IP, user, action).
  4. Correlate — the SIEM applies rules that connect events (e.g., 20 failed logins + 1 success = alert).
  5. Alert — the SIEM creates an alert with a severity and sends it to the SOC queue.
  6. Store and retain — logs are kept for investigations and compliance (often 90 days online, 1 year archived).

Key Log Fields

FieldWhy It Matters
Timestamp + time zoneBuilds the timeline; confirm the time zone (Philippines = UTC+8)
Host / device nameIdentifies the affected asset
Source and destination IP/portShows who talked to whom; distinguishes ingress vs egress
User accountShows who did it — or whose account was misused
Process / file / hashIdentifies the program involved
Action / resultAllowed, blocked, quarantined, failed
Rule / signature name and severityWhy the tool raised the alert and how serious it thinks it is

Sample Firewall Log Line

2026-11-04 10:15:22 FW-01 action=DENY proto=TCP src=192.0.2.8:51234 dst=203.0.113.10:3389 rule=Block-RDP-Inbound

Each security solution has a management console where analysts see alerts, endpoint status, and actions. Examples: Microsoft Defender portal, Wazuh dashboard, firewall web GUI, and SIEM search interfaces. In each console, learn where to find: the alert list, device/agent status, detection details, actions taken, and logs.

Security solutions assign a severity to each alert. Vendors use different scales, so SOPs map them to a common scale.

Common ScaleTypical Vendor ValuesMeaningExample
CriticalCritical / 13–15 (Wazuh) / P1Active, high-impact threat; act immediatelyRansomware encrypting files
HighHigh / 10–12 / P2Likely compromise needing urgent actionMalware executing, not yet contained
MediumMedium / 7–9 / P3Suspicious activity needing reviewPort scan from the internet
LowLow / 4–6 / P4Minor or blocked activityAdware blocked by AV
InformationalInfo / 0–3Normal events for recordsSuccessful signature update
TIP
A tool's severity is a starting point, not the final answer. A "Low" alert on the domain controller may matter more than a "Medium" alert on a test PC. You will learn to assess alerts against pre-identified criteria on Day 6.

TermMeaning
Defense in depthUsing multiple security layers so one failure does not expose everything
SIEMPlatform that collects, normalizes and correlates logs to generate alerts
EDR / XDREndpoint-focused / extended (multi-source) detection and response
WAFFirewall that inspects web application requests
NormalizationConverting different log formats into common fields
Correlation ruleSIEM logic that links several events into one alert
